title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Cassandra
summary: Cassandra is a masterless, AP, wide-column NoSQL database originally open-sourced by Facebook in 2008 (built on Amazon's Dynamo paper and Google's Bigtable paper), designed for linear horizontal scalability and continuous…
objectives: Why is Cassandra called "masterless" and what does that buy you?
What is the difference between partition key, clustering key, and primary key in Cassandra?
What is tunable consistency and how do you choose a consistency level?
How does Cassandra's gossip protocol work, and why is phi accrual detection better than a fixed timeout?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Cassandra is a **masterless, AP, wide-column NoSQL database** originally open-sourced by Facebook in 2008 (built on Amazon's Dynamo paper and Google's Bigtable paper), designed for **linear horizontal scalability** and **continuous availability** with no single point of failure. Each node in a Cassandra cluster is **equal** — there's no primary, no leader, no coordinator election; clients can write to any node, and that node acts as the **coordinator** for the request, forwarding it to the replicas responsible for the partition key (determined by hashing the key with the **Murmur3 partitioner** and mapping the hash onto a **token ring**). Data is replicated to N nodes (the **replication factor**) using **replication strategies** (SimpleStrategy for single-DC, NetworkTopologyStrategy for multi-DC). Cassandra exposes **tunable consistency** — every read/write specifies a consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL) — letting the developer trade latency against correctness per query. Storage uses an **LSM tree** (memtable + immutable SSTables on disk) with **compaction strategies** (Size-Tiered, Leveled, Time-Window) controlling read amplification vs. write amplification. Cluster membership and failure detection use a **gossip protocol** — every node gossips with random peers every second to learn the cluster state, with **phi accrual failure detectors** for robust "is this node dead?" decisions.

Cassandra's defining trait is its **masterless architecture**. There's no leader node, no ZooKeeper-style coordinator, no failover election — every node is identical and can serve any request. When a client connects to any node (called the **coordinator** for that request) with a write, the coordinator hashes the partition key with Murmur3 (a fast non-cryptographic hash), maps the hash onto a 64-bit token ring, identifies the N nodes responsible for that token range (the **replicas**), and forwards the write to all of them in parallel. As soon as the requested consistency level (e.g., QUORUM = `floor(N/2)+1`) of replicas ack, the coordinator returns success to the client. If a replica is down or slow, the coordinator stashes a **hint** locally and replays it when the replica recovers — a feature called **hinted handoff**. This design means Cassandra has **no failover downtime** — losing any node just routes around it. Real-world: Netflix runs 300+ Cassandra nodes across three AWS regions; killing any node (or even a whole AZ) doesn't impact availability. Apple runs a 75,000-node Cassandra cluster for iMessage and iCloud — the largest known NoSQL deployment — precisely because adding nodes is trivial (start a new node, it joins the ring, takes ownership of token ranges via **bootstrapping**, and streams data from neighbors).

The **partitioner** is the function that maps a partition key to a token on the ring. Cassandra 1.2+ defaults to **Murmur3Partitioner** (a 64-bit Murmur hash), which distributes keys uniformly across the ring — critical for avoiding hot spots. The older RandomPartitioner used MD5 (slower, 128-bit). The deprecated ByteOrderedPartitioner preserved lexical ordering (so range queries on keys worked) but caused severe hot-spotting (a single sequential-write workload funnels to one node) — it's almost never used in production. The **token ring** is a circular 64-bit integer space (from -2^63 to +2^63-1); each node owns one or more **token ranges** (segments of the ring). A partition key like `user_42` hashes to, say, token `0x4F3A...`, which falls in node 3's range — node 3 (and its replicas) own that partition. In a 6-node cluster with RF=3, each node owns 1/6 of the ring and replicates to the next 2 nodes clockwise (giving 3 copies total). **Vnodes** (virtual nodes, default 256 per node) replace single-token-per-node with many small ranges per node — this makes cluster rebalancing trivial (a new node takes vnodes from many existing nodes evenly, rather than streaming one giant range from one neighbor).

**Tunable consistency** is Cassandra's killer feature. Every read/write specifies a **consistency level**:
- `ONE` — wait for 1 replica (fastest, may return stale data)
- `TWO` / `THREE` — wait for 2 or 3 replicas
- `QUORUM` — wait for `floor(N/2)+1` replicas (strong consistency if R+W > N)
- `LOCAL_QUORUM` — wait for quorum in the local DC only (multi-DC, low latency)
- `EACH_QUORUM` — quorum in every DC (strongest, slowest)
- `ALL` — wait for all replicas (lose any node, fail the request)
- `LOCAL_ONE` — one replica in local DC (multi-DC, low latency)

The classic formula: **if R + W > N, reads see the latest write** (strong consistency). With N=3, QUORUM reads + QUORUM writes means R=2, W=2, R+W=4 > 3 → strong. With ONE + ONE, R=1, W=1, R+W=2 < 3 → eventually consistent (you may read stale data right after a write). Real-world: Netflix uses `LOCAL_QUORUM` for user-history writes (must be durable in the local DC, don't wait for cross-DC latency) and `LOCAL_ONE` for reads (fast, eventually consistent is fine since they can tolerate a few seconds of staleness). The trade-off: stronger consistency = more replicas contacted = higher latency. Netflix explicitly chose `LOCAL_QUORUM` over `QUORUM` to avoid paying cross-region latency on every write — they accept that a failover to another region might lose the last few seconds of writes (a deliberate trade-off).

The **gossip protocol** is how Cassandra nodes learn about each other without a central registry. Every second, each node picks 1-3 random peers and sends them its view of the cluster state (which nodes are alive, their tokens, their schema versions, their rack/DC). The recipient merges this with its own view and gossips the merged state forward. Within seconds, the entire cluster converges on a consistent view. **Phi accrual failure detection** is the clever bit — instead of a binary "alive/dead" decision after a fixed timeout, each node maintains a continuous suspicion level (`phi`) for each peer based on the recent inter-arrival time of gossip from that peer. If a peer's gossip arrivals are normally ~1 second apart but suddenly stop, `phi` rises continuously; when it crosses a threshold (default 8, meaning "very unlikely this peer is alive if it were healthy"), the peer is marked down. This adapts to network conditions (a slow link raises the baseline, avoiding false positives). Real-world: Netflix's Chaos Monkey kills Cassandra nodes randomly; gossip + phi detection means the cluster detects and routes around the failure in ~10 seconds with no operator action.

The **LSM tree** storage (Log-Structured Merge tree) is why Cassandra writes are fast. A write goes to: (1) the **commit log** (append-only, fsync'd for durability) and (2) the **memtable** (in-memory sorted structure). The write then acks — no disk seek for the data itself. When the memtable fills (default 128 MB or 1 hour), it's flushed to disk as an immutable **SSTable** (Sorted String Table), and a new memtable starts. Reads merge data from the memtable + multiple SSTables (using Bloom filters to skip SSTables that don't have the key, and an index to find the row in the SSTable that does). Over time, many SSTables accumulate, slowing reads — so Cassandra runs **compaction** in the background to merge them. **Size-tiered compaction** (STCS) merges similarly-sized SSTables — great for write-heavy workloads, but reads may touch many SSTables. **Leveled compaction** (LCS) keeps SSTables in levels where each level is 10× the previous — great for read-heavy workloads (at most one SSTable per level needs to be read), but writes are amplified (each write is rewritten ~10× as it propagates through levels). **Time-window compaction** (TWCS) is purpose-built for time-series — each time window (e.g., 1 day) becomes one SSTable, and old windows are simply dropped when they expire. Real-world: Netflix uses TWCS for viewing history (drop data older than 90 days by simply dropping the SSTable — no tombstones, no compaction overhead).

**Tombstones** are Cassandra's deletion mechanism — because SSTables are immutable, you can't actually delete a row; instead, you write a tombstone marker that supersedes the live data. Reads skip tombstoned data, but the tombstone stays until compaction removes it. This is a critical operational concern: if you write and delete many rows rapidly (e.g., a queue-like workload), tombstones accumulate and reads slow down — the famous "tombstone overflow" problem. The fix is `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days, after which tombstones are eligible for compaction) and avoiding Cassandra for queue workloads. This is why people say **"Cassandra is great for writes, not deletes."**

Real-world: **Instagram** uses Cassandra to store 2 billion+ users' feeds. Each user's feed is a partition keyed by `user_id`, with `post_id` as the clustering key (sorted by timestamp). A new post from someone you follow is a write to your feed partition — billions of writes per day, but each write is a single-partition write (fast). Reads are "give me the latest 50 posts for user X" — a single-partition range scan, sub-10ms. The trade-off: a single user's feed can't exceed ~2 GB (the partition size limit); popular followees with millions of followers fan out millions of writes per post (the "celebrity problem"), solved by hybrid approaches (lazy fan-out for celebrities). Apple's 75k-node iMessage cluster is the canonical "scale test" — it handles hundreds of millions of concurrent conversations, with each conversation as a partition, replicated across DCs for HA. The lesson: Cassandra shines for **write-heavy, time-series or partition-keyed workloads** where you can model queries as "give me the latest N for this partition key." It struggles for ad-hoc queries (no JOINs, limited secondary indexes) and deletes.

+ next 2 replicas (RF=3)"| Replicas Replicas --> N1["Node 1 (replica 1)"] Replicas --> N2["Node 2 (replica 2)"] Replicas --> N3["Node 3 (replica 3)"] N1 --> CL1["Commit log (fsync)
+ Memtable (in-memory)"] N2 --> CL2["Commit log + Memtable"] N3 --> CL3["Commit log + Memtable"] N1 -->|"ack"| Coord N2 -->|"ack"| Coord Coord -->|"quorum reached -> ack client"| Client CL1 -.->|"memtable flush"| SST1["SSTable-1 (immutable)"] SST1 -.->|"compaction"| SST2["SSTable-2 (merged)"] Goss["Gossip (every 1s)"] <-->|"peer state"| N1 Goss <--> N2 Goss <--> N3 Goss --> Phi["Phi accrual detector
(suspicion level)"] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Token ring (RF=3, 6 nodes, vnodes simplified): N1 (tokens -2^63..-1.3*2^62) .--+--. / \ N6 / \ N2 ---+ +--- \ / \ / N5 '--+--' N3 N4 Write key "user_42": 1. hash("user_42") with Murmur3 -> 0x4F3A... 2. token 0x4F3A falls in N2's range 3. RF=3 -> replicate to N2, N3, N4 (next 2 clockwise) 4. CL=LOCAL_QUORUM (in local DC) -> wait for 2 of 3 acks 5. N2,N3 ack -> client gets success Write path (per replica): write -> commit log (fsync for durability) -> memtable (in-memory sorted) -> ack coordinator Memtable flush (when full or 1h elapsed): memtable -> SSTable-001 (immutable on disk) Read path: read key k -> check memtable -> check Bloom filter for each SSTable -> read from SSTables that match -> merge (latest wins by timestamp) -> row cache (optional) Compaction (background): many SSTables -> merged SSTable (fewer, bigger) - STCS: merge similar-sized (write-heavy) - LCS: leveled, 1 SSTable per level (read-heavy) - TWCS: one SSTable per time window (time-series) Gossip (every 1s): N1 picks 2 random peers (e.g., N3, N5) sends: "I'm alive, my token ranges, my schema ver, ..." receives: peer's view of cluster merges -> updates local view Convergence: O(log N) seconds for full cluster Phi failure detection: normal inter-gossip arrival = 1s last seen 5s ago -> phi = 4.2 (suspicious) last seen 10s ago -> phi = 8.0 (mark DOWN) (continuous value, adapts to network conditions) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client driver connects to any Cassandra node (the **coordinator**) and sends a write with a partition key and a consistency level (e.g., `LOCAL_QUORUM`). The coordinator hashes the partition key with Murmur3 to find the token on the 64-bit ring, identifies the N replicas (RF=3 means the token's owning node plus the next 2 clockwise on the ring), and forwards the write to all replicas in parallel. Each replica appends to its commit log (fsync'd) and inserts into its memtable (in-memory), then acks. The coordinator returns success once the consistency level is met (e.g., 2 of 3 for LOCAL_QUORUM). 2. In the background, each replica flushes full memtables to immutable SSTables on disk. Reads merge memtable + relevant SSTables (skipping SSTables via Bloom filter). Compaction merges SSTables to control read amplification. Gossip runs continuously so all nodes know the cluster state; phi accrual detection marks unreachable nodes DOWN after ~10 seconds, and the coordinator routes around them (using hinted handoff to deliver missed writes when they recover). 3. Tunable consistency per query lets developers trade latency for correctness: `LOCAL_ONE` for fast eventually-consistent reads (analytics), `LOCAL_QUORUM` for durable writes that survive a single-node failure within the DC, `EACH_QUORUM` for the strongest cross-DC guarantees (slowest). The formula R+W > N guarantees strong consistency; for RF=3, QUORUM reads + QUORUM writes (R=2, W=2, R+W=4 > 3) gives linearizability for a single partition.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Cassandra feature mock: gossip + token ring + tunable consistency.
- Cheap hash stand-in for Murmur3Partitioner (returns 64-bit).
- Simulate a down node coming back; replay hints.
- Find first node with token >= tok, then take next RF-1 clockwise
- Hinted handoff: stash write for later replay
- Repair in background (read repair) by writing newest back
- Kill a node, still succeed with QUORUM
- Write to a key whose replicas include the dead node (hint stashed)

**Defines:** `murmur3()`, `Node`, `Cluster`

```python
"""
Cassandra feature mock: gossip + token ring + tunable consistency.

Demonstrates: Murmur3-style partitioning, RF replication,
coordinator forwarding, consistency levels (ONE/QUORUM/ALL),
hinted handoff for down nodes, and phi-style failure detection.
Pure stdlib, runnable.
"""
import hashlib, random, time
from collections import defaultdict

def murmur3(token: str) -> int:
    """Cheap hash stand-in for Murmur3Partitioner (returns 64-bit)."""
    h = hashlib.md5(token.encode()).hexdigest()
    return int(h[:16], 16) - (1 << 63)   # signed 64-bit

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name: str, token: int):
        self.name = name
        self.token = token
        self.alive = True
        self.data: dict[str, dict] = {}        # partition_key -> rows
        self.hints: dict[str, list] = {}       # down_node -> [(key, val)]
        self.last_seen = time.time()

    def write(self, key: str, val: dict) -> None:
        self.data[key] = val
        self.last_seen = time.time()

    def read(self, key: str):
        return self.data.get(key)

class Cluster:
    def __init__(self, rf: int = 3):
        self.nodes: list[Node] = []
        self.rf = rf

    def add(self, node: Node) -> None:
        self.nodes.append(node)
        self.nodes.sort(key=lambda n: n.token)

    def replicas_for(self, key: str) -> list[Node]:
        tok = murmur3(key)
        # find first node with token >= tok, then take next RF-1 clockwise
        for i, n in enumerate(self.nodes):
            if n.token >= tok:
                start = i
                break
        else:
            start = 0
        return [self.nodes[(start + j) % len(self.nodes)] for j in range(self.rf)]

    def write(self, key: str, val: dict, cl: str = "QUORUM") -> bool:
        replicas = self.replicas_for(key)
        acks = 0
        for r in replicas:
            if r.alive:
                r.write(key, val)
                acks += 1
            else:
                # hinted handoff: stash write for later replay
                self._coordinator.hints.setdefault(r.name, []).append((key, val))
        needed = {"ONE": 1, "QUORUM": len(replicas) // 2 + 1,
                  "ALL": len(replicas)}[cl]
        return acks >= needed

    def read(self, key: str, cl: str = "QUORUM"):
        replicas = self.replicas_for(key)
        results = []
        for r in replicas:
            if r.alive:
                v = r.read(key)
                if v is not None:
                    results.append(v)
        needed = {"ONE": 1, "QUORUM": len(replicas) // 2 + 1,
                  "ALL": len(replicas)}[cl]
        if len(results) < needed:
            return None
        # repair in background (read repair) by writing newest back
        return results[0]

    def recover(self, name: str) -> None:
        """Simulate a down node coming back; replay hints."""
        for n in self.nodes:
            if n.name == name:
                n.alive = True
                for key, val in self._coordinator.hints.get(name, []):
                    n.write(key, val)
                self._coordinator.hints.pop(name, None)

# --- demo ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    cluster = Cluster(rf=3)
    cluster._coordinator = type("C", (), {"hints": {}})()  # tiny shim
    for i in range(6):
        cluster.add(Node(f"N{i}", random.randint(-(1<<62), 1<<62)))

    print("Ring:", [(n.name, n.token) for n in cluster.nodes])

    # write with QUORUM
    print("write alice ->", cluster.write("user:alice",
          {"name": "Alice", "score": 100}, cl="QUORUM"))
    print("write bob   ->", cluster.write("user:bob",
          {"name": "Bob", "score": 50}, cl="QUORUM"))

    # kill a node, still succeed with QUORUM
    victim = cluster.replicas_for("user:alice")[0]
    victim.alive = False
    print(f"\nKilled {victim.name}")
    print("read alice (QUORUM after node down):",
          cluster.read("user:alice", cl="QUORUM"))

    # write to a key whose replicas include the dead node (hint stashed)
    print("write carol (with one replica down) ->",
          cluster.write("user:carol", {"name": "Carol"}, cl="ONE"))

    # node recovers, hint replayed
    cluster.recover(victim.name)
    print(f"After {victim.name} recovered, its data:",
          victim.data.get("user:carol"))
```

quiz.question: Why is Cassandra called "masterless" and what does that buy you?
options: B-tree** (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) does in-place updates — to change a row, the engine reads the disk page, modifies it, writes it back.
Every Cassandra read/write specifies a consistency level (CL) — how many replicas must respond before the operation is considered successful.
NetworkTopologyStrategy (NTS) is rack/DC-aware — you specify RF per DC (e.g., {'us-east': 3, 'us-west': 3, 'eu-west': 3}).
Cassandra has no primary, no leader, no coordinator election — every node is equal and can serve any client request.
quiz.explanation: Cassandra has no primary, no leader, no coordinator election — every node is equal and can serve any client request. The first node a client contacts becomes the coordinator for that request; the coordinator hashes the partition key, finds the replicas, and forwards. If the coordinator itself dies, the client just connects to a different node.

quiz.question: What is the difference between partition key, clustering key, and primary key in Cassandra?
options: Every Cassandra read/write specifies a consistency level (CL) — how many replicas must respond before the operation is considered successful.
Cassandra offers three compaction strategies: (1) Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) — merges similarly-sized SSTables into a bigger one when there are min_threshold (default 4) of them.
NetworkTopologyStrategy (NTS) is rack/DC-aware — you specify RF per DC (e.g., {'us-east': 3, 'us-west': 3, 'eu-west': 3}).
The primary key in Cassandra is the combination of partition key + clustering key (and optionally static columns).
quiz.explanation: The primary key in Cassandra is the combination of partition key + clustering key (and optionally static columns). The partition key is the first part of the primary key — it determines which node(s) own the row via Murmur3 hashing. All rows with the same partition key live on the same set of replicas (the partition).

Levels: ONE (1 replica, fastest), TWO, THREE, QUORUM (floor(N/2)+1), LOCAL_QUORUM (quorum in local DC only), EACH_QUORUM (quorum in every DC, slowest), ALL (all replicas, fails if any down), LOCAL_ONE, SERIAL/LOCAL_SERIAL (for lightweight transactions using Paxos).

options: Cassandra's data model is query-driven — each table supports one access pattern efficiently.
Cassandra provides counters as a special data type — UPDATE likes SET count = count + 1 WHERE post_id = ? is atomic at the partition level.
When the node comes back online: (1) Gossip marks it UP — within ~10 seconds, peers detect the node responding to gossip and update their state.

The recipient merges this with its own view and gossips the merged state forward. options: Cassandra has no primary, no leader, no coordinator election — every node is equal and can serve any client request.
Use a fan-out-on-write model with the feed table keyed by user_id.
Cassandra provides counters as a special data type — UPDATE likes SET count = count + 1 WHERE post_id = ? is atomic at the partition level.
B-tree** (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) does in-place updates — to change a row, the engine reads the disk page, modifies it, writes it back.
quiz.explanation: B-tree** (used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) does in-place updates — to change a row, the engine reads the disk page, modifies it, writes it back. This causes write amplification (one logical write may rewrite 4-16 KB of disk) and random I/O (each update seeks to a different disk location). Under heavy write load, B-trees become disk-seek-bound.
